summary: Cefotaxime is a third-generation cephalosporin given by IV or IM injection for serious infections caused by susceptible Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms. It is bactericidal through inhibition of bacterial cell-wall synthesis and is generally well tolerated, with local injection reactions being most common.
indications: Lower respiratory tract infections, including pneumonia
Genitourinary infections, including urinary tract infections
Gynecologic infections, including pelvic inflammatory disease, endometritis, and pelvic cellulitis

dosage.t: Continue at least 48-72 h after defervescence
Adjust to severity and organism susceptibility

dosage.n: Add anti-chlamydial cover if C. trachomatis suspected
For contaminated or potentially contaminated surgery

dosage.d: 1 g at cord clamping, then 1 g at 6 and 12 hours
dosage.n: First dose IV as soon as umbilical cord is clamped

dosage.t: Dose by age, not gestational maturity

dosage.c: Infants and children 1 month-12 years (<50 kg)
dosage.t: Use higher end for severe infection or meningitis
dosage.n: Children 50 kg or more use adult dosing, max 12 g/day

admin: Reconstitute before IM or IV administration; shake to dissolve and inspect for particulates and discoloration (solutions range from very pale yellow to light amber)
For IM: reconstitute 500 mg in 2 mL, 1 g in 3 mL, 2 g in 5 mL of diluent
For IV: reconstitute 500 mg, 1 g, or 2 g in 10 mL of diluent
Do NOT give as a rapid (<60 second) bolus through a central venous catheter - risk of life-threatening arrhythmia
Continue therapy at least 48-72 hours after defervescence or eradication; treat Group A streptococcal infections for a minimum of 10 days
Do not exceed 12 g per day
moa: Cefotaxime is a bactericidal beta-lactam that binds penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis. It remains active in the presence of many penicillinases and cephalosporinases, and its desacetyl metabolite contributes to antibacterial activity.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to cefotaxime sodium or to the cephalosporin class
relative: Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity to penicillin - use with caution
Any history of significant drug allergy
History of gastrointestinal disease, particularly colitis
monitor: Hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis - discontinue and treat if reaction occurs
Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, which may appear up to 2 months after therapy
Renal function, especially with concurrent nephrotoxic drugs or in the elderly
Hematologic effects (neutropenia, leukopenia, eosinophilia) with prolonged use
Arrhythmia risk with rapid central-line bolus injection

preg: Animal reproduction studies in mice and rats (up to ~0.4-0.8 times the human dose by body surface area) showed no embryotoxicity or teratogenicity. Cefotaxime crosses the placenta and appears in cord blood, but the human fetal effect is unknown and there are no well-controlled studies; use during pregnancy only if clearly needed.
lact: Cefotaxime is excreted in human milk in low concentrations; exercise caution when administering to a nursing woman.
renal: High and prolonged serum levels can occur with reduced urine output, so reduce the total daily dose in renal insufficiency. In patients with estimated creatinine clearance below 20 mL/min/1.73 m2, halve the dose; further adjustment depends on degree of impairment, infection severity, and organism susceptibility.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is required; transient elevations of AST, ALT, LDH, and alkaline phosphatase may occur.

moderate: Probenecid - reduces renal clearance of cefotaxime by ~50% and raises plasma levels; avoid cefotaxime doses above 6 g/day with probenecid
interactions.food: Not applicable; cefotaxime is administered parenterally.
interactions.alcohol: No disulfiram-like reaction was observed when cefotaxime was given with ethanol.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause a positive direct Coombs test and a false-positive urine glucose with copper-reduction tests (Benedict's/Fehling's/CLINITEST); use enzyme-based glucose tests instead.

serious: Transient elevations of hepatic enzymes and BUN
rare: Reversible encephalopathy with high beta-lactam doses
emergency: Anaphylaxis or serious hypersensitivity reaction (may need epinephrine)
Potentially life-threatening arrhythmia after rapid (<60 second) central-line bolus
Fulminant or fatal C. difficile colitis

monitoring: Renal function (BUN, creatinine), especially with nephrotoxic co-medications or in the elderly
Complete blood count during prolonged therapy
Bowel pattern for C. difficile diarrhea
counsel: This antibiotic treats bacterial, not viral, infections such as the common cold
Complete the full prescribed course even if feeling better to avoid resistance and treatment failure
Report watery or bloody diarrhea (with or without cramps or fever), even up to 2 months after treatment
Tell your clinician about any prior allergic reactions to cephalosporins, penicillins, or other drugs
Local discomfort at the injection site is common
pearls: Third-generation cephalosporin with broad Gram-negative cover but no activity against Chlamydia trachomatis or enterococci
Never give as a rapid central-venous bolus - fatal arrhythmias have been reported
Halve the dose when creatinine clearance is below 20 mL/min/1.73 m2
Most ESBL- and carbapenemase-producing isolates are resistant; the desacetyl metabolite adds to bactericidal activity
missed: Cefotaxime is given by a healthcare provider on a fixed schedule; if a scheduled dose is delayed, give it as soon as possible and adjust subsequent timing rather than doubling, maintaining the prescribed interval.
overdose: Overdose has usually produced no overt toxicity, most often transient rises in BUN and creatinine; high beta-lactam doses carry a risk of reversible encephalopathy. There is no specific antidote. Observe the patient carefully and provide supportive care; hemodialysis may help remove the drug in severe renal compromise.
